title: Test Bank · Ch. 4
description: Johns & Saks chapter test bank, Ch. 4 (Values, Attitudes & Work Behaviour): multiple-choice and true/false items, each key re-checked against the 12th-edition text.

questions.prompt: In which of the following is work viewed as most important and central in life?
questions.explanation: **Japan** topped the work-centrality survey. Belgians and Americans were average and the British scored low, so the other countries listed are not the highest.

questions.prompt: According to Geert Hofstede's research, the most masculine culture is that of
questions.explanation: In Hofstede's research **Japan** (tied with Slovakia) is the most masculine society, while the Scandinavian countries are the most feminine. Canada is mid-pack and the United States is fairly masculine.

questions.prompt: According to Geert Hofstede's research, the most individualistic culture is that of
questions.explanation: The **United States** is among the most individualistic societies. Venezuela, Colombia and Pakistan are among the most collective, and Japan falls mid-pack.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the cultural value of power distance is FALSE?

options.text: Japan has higher power distance than Canada.
Superiors tend to be accessible in low power distance cultures.
In high power distance cultures the unequal distribution of power is acceptable to members of the culture.
Denmark has lower power distance than Mexico.
High power distance cultures tend to also be individualistic, rather than collective, cultures.

questions.explanation: High power distance cultures tend to be **collectivistic**, not individualistic; individualistic cultures downplay power differences. The other statements match the text, including Japan being higher than Canada.

questions.prompt: In a collective culture

options.text: it may be a good idea to reward groups rather than individuals.
loyalty to one's family or clan is downplayed.
privacy and personal initiative are stressed.
power distance tends to be low.

questions.explanation: In collective cultures people favour interdependence and loyalty to family or clan, so it may make sense to **reward groups rather than individuals**. Privacy and personal initiative are individualistic values.

questions.prompt: In Geert Hofstede's survey of values across cultures, individualistic societies can be contrasted most readily with __________ societies.
questions.explanation: Hofstede's dimension is **individualism versus collectivism**, so individualistic societies contrast with collective ones. Masculine and power distance are separate dimensions.

questions.prompt: Discrepancy theory suggests that job dissatisfaction develops when

options.text: supervisors and employees differ radically in their values.
workers don't see their jobs as offering what they want.
job outcomes don't match job inputs.
workers begin to take benefits for granted.

questions.explanation: **Discrepancy theory** says satisfaction depends on the gap between the job outcomes people want and the outcomes they perceive they obtain. Comparing inputs and outcomes is equity theory, not discrepancy theory.

questions.prompt: What job satisfaction facet is most likely to stimulate high performance?
questions.explanation: Satisfaction with the **content of the work itself** is the facet most likely to stimulate performance, since interesting, challenging, meaningful jobs matter most. Pay is a common but weaker guess.

questions.prompt: If a manager wants to increase the job satisfaction of employees, he should

options.text: give employees the job outcomes that they want.

questions.explanation: When good performance is followed by **rewards**, employees are more likely to be satisfied. Blanket pay raises are not tied to performance, so they miss the mechanism the text describes.

source.note: Option d reworded so it excludes the reverse link; the text says each can influence the other.

questions.prompt: The contemporary view of the relationship between job satisfaction and performance suggests that

options.text: job satisfaction and performance are not related.
performance contributes to job satisfaction and job satisfaction contributes to performance.
job satisfaction contributes to performance, but performance does not contribute to job satisfaction.
job satisfaction and performance are impossible to measure adequately.

questions.explanation: The text says satisfaction contributes to performance, but **performance can also contribute to satisfaction** when it is rewarded. The relationship runs both ways, although satisfaction is the more likely cause.

questions.prompt: Alice perceives her job inputs as high and her job outcomes as high. Alice perceives Jane's inputs as low and her outcomes as low. Jane's perceptions are identical to Alice's in all respects. According to equity theory

options.text: Jane experiences inequity but Alice doesn't.
both women should earn exactly the same income.
Alice experiences inequity but Jane doesn't.

questions.explanation: **Equity** exists when each person's outcome/input ratio matches the comparison person's. Both women see their own ratio as equal to the other's (high/high versus low/low), so both feel equity.

questions.prompt: Attitudes are a function of

options.text: what we feel and intend to do.
what we obtain and what we want.
what we do and what we want.
what we think and what we feel.
what we think and what we see.

questions.explanation: Attitudes are a function of **what we think (beliefs) and what we feel (values)**. Intentions and what we see are not part of the formula.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements concerning values is FALSE?

options.text: Values are randomly distributed across the population.
Members of different occupational groups tend to hold different values.
Value differences may be responsible for conflict between people from different occupational groups.
Values are learned through reinforcement processes.

questions.explanation: Values are **not randomly distributed**: different groups, such as managers and union officials, hold different values, and values are learned through reinforcement. That makes the random-distribution statement false.

questions.prompt: A fairly stable evaluative tendency to respond consistently to some specific object, situation, person, or category of people is called a(n)
questions.explanation: An **attitude** is a fairly stable evaluative tendency to respond consistently to a specific object, situation, person or group. A value is broader and about general preferences.

questions.prompt: Which of the following equations is accurate?
questions.explanation: **Belief + value = attitude**, and the attitude then influences behaviour. Behaviour is the outcome, not an ingredient, and equity is a ratio of outcomes to inputs.

questions.prompt: Which sequence represents current expert thinking about the relationship among the variables shown?
questions.explanation: The 12th edition says many organizations do not reward good performance enough, so **satisfaction is more likely to affect performance** than the reverse. The older performance-rewards-satisfaction ordering is no longer the 'current thinking'.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th edition now says satisfaction is more likely to drive performance, so this older 'current expert thinking' sequence is no longer the textbook position.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a job input, according to equity theory?
questions.explanation: **Pay is an outcome**, not an input. Inputs are what people give up or offer, such as education, seniority, experience and hard work.

questions.prompt: One reason why two people performing the same job may have different attitudes toward that job is that

options.text: they may differ in their perceptions concerning the actual nature of the job.
they may differ in what they want from the job.
they may have different work values.
they may differ in their beliefs about the job.

questions.explanation: Two people in the same job can differ in **perceptions (beliefs) of the job and in what they want (values)**. All of the listed reasons fit, so all of the above is correct.

questions.prompt: The collection of attitudes that workers have about their jobs is called
questions.explanation: **Job satisfaction** is a collection of attitudes workers have about their jobs. Equity and discrepancy are theories of what drives it.

questions.prompt: Mark says that he is happy with his salary, but finds that his job is not very challenging. This illustrates the concept of
questions.explanation: Being happy with salary but not the challenge shows **facet satisfaction**: different attitudes toward separate facets of the job. Fairness concepts are about outcomes, process and communication.

questions.prompt: What job satisfaction facets does the Job Descriptive Index measure?
questions.explanation: The Job Descriptive Index measures facet and overall satisfaction; its five facets are work, supervision, people, pay and promotions.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th edition names the Job Descriptive Index but no longer lists its five facets.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true?

options.text: The Job Descriptive Index measures attitudes.
The values held by members of various occupations are remarkably similar.
Indirect communication is more likely to change attitudes than face-to-face persuasion.
Pay is often considered an input in equity theory.
Persuasion that is designed to modify beliefs is usually emotionally oriented.

questions.explanation: The **Job Descriptive Index measures attitudes** (job satisfaction). Pay is an outcome, not an input, and the persuasion and occupational-values statements are not supported by the text.

questions.prompt: All forms of organizational commitment are related to
questions.explanation: **All forms of commitment** reduce turnover intentions and actual turnover. Performance links differ by type: affective helps it, continuance hurts it.

questions.prompt: Which job satisfaction facet is the best predictor of absence from work?
questions.explanation: Satisfaction with the **content of the work** is the best predictor of absenteeism, though the link is weak. Pay is the tempting but wrong facet.

questions.prompt: Tom recently started working at his fifth job in ten years. Tom has been happy at all of these jobs. This suggests that his job satisfaction is

options.text: highest when the employment opportunity is only short term.

questions.explanation: Being satisfied across five different jobs suggests a **dispositional** contribution: satisfaction stays fairly stable even when employers change. It is not explained mainly by situational factors.

questions.prompt: Here is an equity equation for Louis and Rita, both of whom agree that all figures are accurate: Louis has Outcomes = 19 and Inputs = 7; Rita has Outcomes = 10 and Inputs = 5. According to equity theory:

options.text: Rita and Louis should be experiencing job satisfaction.
Louis and Rita should be experiencing equity.

questions.explanation: Rita's ratio is 10/5 = 2 and Louis's is 19/7 = 2.7, so Rita is on the **short end of the stick** and perceives inequity. Louis does not have equity either, and equity is not the same thing as satisfaction.

questions.prompt: In order to predict turnover it would be most useful to know a person's

options.text: satisfaction with various facets of the job.

questions.explanation: **Intentions to quit** are very good predictors of actual turnover. Satisfaction and commitment affect turnover mainly through intentions.

questions.prompt: Job satisfaction research has pointed to the influence of dispositional factors because

options.text: optimists with realistic thinking processes are more likely to be satisfied.
job satisfaction is stable over time, regardless of current employer.
identical twins raised apart tend to have similar levels of job satisfaction.
adolescent dispositional measures correlate with job satisfaction.

questions.explanation: Twins raised apart, stability across employers, and adolescent disposition all point to **dispositional influences** on satisfaction. Because every listed finding supports it, all of the above is correct.

questions.prompt: Carefully applying equity theory should have a direct effect upon
questions.explanation: Equity theory is about outcome/input comparisons, so it bears most directly on **distributive fairness**, the fairness of what people receive. Procedural and interactional fairness are about process and communication.

questions.prompt: Organizational citizenship behaviour

options.text: is positively related to job satisfaction.
involves carrying out one's assigned job duties to the best of one's ability.
is usually rewarded through formal performance evaluations.
is an important evaluation component in most formal performance review systems.

questions.explanation: **OCB** is positively related to job satisfaction. Doing one's assigned duties is ordinary task performance, and OCB is usually not captured by formal evaluations.

questions.prompt: Distributive fairness results in
questions.explanation: Distributive fairness is about receiving the outcomes you think you deserve, which is what the **equity** comparison tests. It does not produce procedural fairness, which concerns the process.

questions.prompt: Organizational citizenship behaviour is

options.text: one of Geert Hofstede's work-related value dimensions.
unlikely to be rewarded directly and explicitly by the organization.
likely to occur when employees experience inequity.

questions.explanation: OCB is voluntary and informal, so it is **unlikely to be rewarded directly and explicitly** by the evaluation system. It is not in job descriptions and is related to satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would not be part of an equity equation involving you and your co-worker Darlene?
questions.explanation: The equity ratio compares **outcomes to inputs** for you and the other person. 'Outputs' is not one of the terms.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pieces of advice is probably least sensible or logical?
questions.explanation: Attitudes come from beliefs and values, so changing beliefs or values changes attitudes. **Values shape attitudes, not the other way round**, so changing attitudes to change values makes least sense.

questions.prompt: To increase organizational citizenship behaviour
questions.explanation: **Job satisfaction** contributes strongly to OCB, especially through fairness. Reduced commitment or fairness would lower OCB.

questions.prompt: To increase the overall job satisfaction of an employee

options.text: create a discrepancy between desired and actual outcomes.

questions.explanation: Overall satisfaction is an average or total of the attitudes toward the job's facets, so raising **facet satisfaction** raises it. A wanted-versus-received discrepancy lowers satisfaction.

questions.prompt: What factor would be most likely to boost continuance commitment?
questions.explanation: A **generous pension fund** is a 'side bet' that raises the cost of leaving, which builds continuance commitment. Interesting work builds affective commitment instead.

questions.prompt: People with the following personality traits tend to be more satisfied with their jobs:
questions.explanation: People who are **extraverted and conscientious** tend to be more satisfied; those high in neuroticism are less satisfied.

questions.prompt: What are emotions?

options.text: Intense, often short-lived, feelings caused by a particular event.
Intense, often long-lived, feelings caused by a particular event.

questions.explanation: **Emotions** are intense, often short-lived feelings caused by a particular event. Moods are less intense, longer-lived and more diffuse.

questions.prompt: What are moods?

options.text: Not so intense, long-lived, diffuse feelings.
Not so intense, long-lived, feelings caused by a particular event.
Intense, often short-lived, feelings caused by a particular event.
Not so intense, often short-lived, diffuse feelings.

questions.explanation: **Moods** are less intense, longer-lived and more diffuse feelings, with no single triggering event. Feelings caused by a particular event are emotions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of affect events theory and job satisfaction?

options.text: The tendency for job satisfaction to spread between people or throughout a group.
When certain "shocks" such as an unsolicited job offer lowers one's job satisfaction and leads to turnover.
Seeing a co-worker being put down by a manager provokes emotional anger and lowers one's job satisfaction.
Seeing a co-worker receiving more outcomes even though your inputs are greater lowers one's job satisfaction.
The tendency for people to conform to certain "display rules" in their job satisfaction in spite of their mood or emotions.

questions.explanation: **Affective events theory** says work events provoke emotions that change satisfaction, such as seeing a co-worker berated by a manager. The equity example involves comparison, not emotion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of emotional contagion?

options.text: When an employee's emotions are in a constant state of change.
Pleasant service encounters contribute to the service provider's satisfaction as well as to that of the customer.
An employee who has low satisfaction at work will also have low satisfaction outside of work.
An employee who is angry at work is also angry at home.
All employees must do certain things in spite of their true mood and emotions to provide pleasant service encounters.

questions.explanation: **Emotional contagion** is the spread of moods and emotions between people, as when pleasant service encounters lift both the provider and the customer. Following display rules is emotional labour.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition term: emotional labour.

questions.prompt: The requirement for people to conform to certain "display rules" in their job behaviour in spite of their true mood or emotions is known as
questions.explanation: **Emotional labour** is the requirement to follow display rules regardless of true mood. Contagion is the spread of moods, and affective events theory explains how events shape satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following jobs are especially laden with display rules?
questions.explanation: Service roles such as **waiters, bank tellers and flight attendants** are especially laden with display rules. Dishwashers and cooks have little customer contact.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition term: emotional labour.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of emotional labour?

options.text: Employees are supposed to repress their anger when dealing with customers.
Employees are supposed to be nice to customers even when they are angry at them.
Employees are supposed to be perky and upbeat even when they feel down.
Employees are supposed to remain calm and civil even when hassled or insulted.

questions.explanation: Each example, whether exaggerating positive emotions or suppressing negative ones, is **emotional labour**: conforming to display rules despite one's true feelings.

questions.prompt: According to the model of employee turnover in the text, what contributes to turnover intentions?

options.text: Job satisfaction, organizational commitment, and mentally challenging work.
Job satisfaction, mentally challenging work, and "shocks."
Mentally challenging work, adequate compensation, and career opportunities.
Mentally challenging work, supervision, and adequate compensation.

questions.explanation: In the turnover model, **job satisfaction, organizational commitment and shocks** contribute to turnover intentions. Challenging work is a contributor to satisfaction, not a separate path.

questions.prompt: According to the model of employee turnover in the text, what two factors are directly related to turnover?

options.text: Job satisfaction and comparison of alternatives.
Turnover intentions and comparison of alternatives.

questions.explanation: In the model, **turnover intentions and comparison of alternatives** feed directly into turnover. Satisfaction and commitment work indirectly through intentions.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between employee job satisfaction, customer satisfaction, and organizational profitability?

options.text: Employee job satisfaction is related to customer satisfaction and organizational profitability.
Employee job satisfaction is related to customer satisfaction but not organizational profitability.
Employee job satisfaction is related to organizational profitability but not customer satisfaction.
Employee job satisfaction is not related to customer satisfaction or organizational profitability.
Employee job satisfaction is not related to customer satisfaction, but customer satisfaction is related to organizational profitability.

questions.explanation: Employee satisfaction is **translated into customer satisfaction and organizational profitability**, as the Maplewave example and 100 Best Companies returns suggest.

questions.prompt: An organization has a safety problem and wants to change employee attitudes towards safety. If they want to focus on changing values, what should they do?

options.text: Tell employees that wearing safety equipment is required by the workers' health and safety board.
Tell employees about a dead worker's family who are suffering because of unsafe work practices.
Tell employees that if they continue to ignore safety rules they will be fired.
Tell employees that employees at other organizations are required to abide by the same safety regulations.
Tell employees that hard hats and safety glasses are not uncomfortable.

questions.explanation: Persuasion aimed at values uses emotional appeals, such as a grieving family's story.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: Persuasion strategies for changing values and beliefs are not covered in the 12th edition chapter.

questions.prompt: What is a communicator trying to modify when he/she uses persuasion to try to change people's attitudes?
questions.explanation: Persuasion changes attitudes by targeting the beliefs and values that form them.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: Persuasion strategies for changing attitudes are not covered in the 12th edition chapter.

questions.prompt: An organization has a safety problem and wants to change employee attitudes towards safety. If they want to focus on changing beliefs, what should they do?

options.text: Tell employees about a dead worker's family who are suffering because of unsafe work practices.
Tell employees about the children who are growing up without parents because of unsafe working behaviour.
Tell employees that hard hats and safety glasses are not uncomfortable.
Tell employees about workers who have been injured because of unsafe work practices and are unable to work and support their families.
Tell employees about workers who have lost limbs due to unsafe work practices.

questions.explanation: Persuasion aimed at beliefs uses factual, rational claims, such as that safety gear is not uncomfortable.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: Persuasion strategies for changing beliefs are not covered in the 12th edition chapter.

questions.prompt: What is interactional fairness?

options.text: When employees have interactions with their managers that they perceive to be fair
When people feel that they have received respectful and informative communication about some outcome
When people see the process used to determine outcomes as reasonable
When people receive what they think they deserve from their jobs
When employees have interactions with each other that they perceive to be fair

questions.explanation: **Interactional fairness** is receiving respectful and informative communication about an outcome. Reasonable processes are procedural fairness, and deserved outcomes are distributive fairness.

questions.prompt: If you experience procedural unfairness at work, how will this affect your satisfaction?

options.text: you will be dissatisfied with the system
you will be dissatisfied with your coworkers
you will be dissatisfied with your pay
you will be dissatisfied with your job
you will be dissatisfied with your boss

questions.explanation: People who experience procedural unfairness are frustrated with the **system**. Interactional unfairness, by contrast, is aimed at the boss.

questions.prompt: If you experience interactional unfairness at work, how will this affect your satisfaction?

options.text: you will be dissatisfied with your friends
you will be dissatisfied with your coworkers
you will be dissatisfied with yourself
you will be dissatisfied with your boss
you will be dissatisfied with the system

questions.explanation: People who experience interactional unfairness are more likely to be dissatisfied with the **boss**. Procedural unfairness leads to dissatisfaction with the system.

questions.prompt: As a manager, you have to communicate to employees their work outcomes. You are concerned about interactional fairness, which means that your communication must be:
questions.explanation: Interactional fairness requires communication that is **respectful and informative**. Respectful means sincere and polite; informative means candid, timely and thorough.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most accurate about the negative effects of distributive unfairness?

options.text: the negative effects of distributive unfairness can only be offset by distributive fairness
procedural fairness but not interactional fairness can offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness
interactional fairness but not procedural fairness can offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness
procedural fairness and interactional fairness can offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness
neither procedural fairness nor interactional fairness can offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness

questions.explanation: Both **procedural and interactional fairness** can, to some extent, offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness. So the options saying only one type works, or that neither works, are wrong.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best represents the relationship between personality and job satisfaction?

options.text: people high in self-esteem and neuroticism are less satisfied
people high in self-esteem and external locus of control are more satisfied
people high in self-esteem and neuroticism are more satisfied
people high in self-esteem and internal locus of control are more satisfied
people with internal locus of control and high in neuroticism are more satisfied

questions.explanation: People high in **self-esteem and internal locus of control** are more satisfied with their jobs. Neuroticism lowers satisfaction, and an external locus of control is not linked to higher satisfaction.

questions.prompt: You have two friends who are going to start new jobs after they graduate. Your friend Sasha has always had high self-esteem and your friend Ellen is someone with an external locus of control. How satisfied do you think your friends will be with their new jobs?

options.text: Sasha will be more satisfied than Ellen
they will both have high job satisfaction
it depends on jobs they have
they will both have low job satisfaction
Ellen will be more satisfied than Sasha

questions.explanation: High self-esteem predicts higher satisfaction, while an external locus of control does not, so **Sasha** should be more satisfied than Ellen. Optimistic, proactive people report higher satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following accurately describes the relationship between cognitive demands, pay, and emotional labour?

options.text: occupations with low cognitive demands tend to be paid more when the jobs are high in emotional labour
occupations with low cognitive demands tend to be paid more when the jobs are low in emotional labour
occupations with high cognitive demands tend to be paid more when the jobs are low in emotional labour
occupations with high cognitive demands tend to be paid more when the jobs are high in emotional labour
occupations with high cognitive demands tend to be paid more regardless of the amount of emotional labour involved

questions.explanation: The link between cognitive demands, pay and emotional labour is not covered in the 12th edition, which discusses only emotional labour's toll on satisfaction and stress.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The cognitive-demands and pay finding on emotional labour is not in the 12th edition.

questions.prompt: What explains the connection between job satisfaction and good attendance?

options.text: the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate people's ability to come to work
the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate mental health and satisfaction with life
the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate people's motivation to come to work
the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate people's experience of positive emotions
the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate people's desire to want to come to work

questions.explanation: The 12th edition explains the weak absence link through constraints, such as illness and attendance policies, and does not give this mental-health explanation.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: This explanation of the satisfaction-attendance link is not in the 12th edition, which lists constraints on absence instead.

questions.prompt: You have three friends who have been working since they graduated. Tom has the best paying job. Kamal has the most challenging job. Leanne has the least stressful job. Which friend(s) is least likely to be absent from work?
questions.explanation: Satisfaction with the **content of the work** is the best predictor of absence, so the friend with the most challenging job, Kamal, is least likely to be absent. Pay and low stress are not the key facet.

questions.prompt: Your three best friends all found jobs after graduation. Jack has just found out that he has to attend a training program. Jamal has just announced that he is getting a divorce. And Jenna is complaining about her boss who has been pushing her to work harder. Which friend(s) is most likely to quit?
questions.explanation: A marital breakup is a **shock** that can prompt quitting even when satisfaction is unaffected. A training program is not a shock, and Jenna's boss problem is only one dissatisfaction.

questions.prompt: Which one of your friends is experiencing a "honeymoon effect"?

options.text: Thelma has just quit a job that had many things she did not like, started a new job with many things she likes, and does not yet know about some other things she will not like
Luke has just quit a job that had many things he did not like, started a new job with many things he likes, and knows there will be even more good things to come
Jenna has just returned home from her honeymoon and now must begin her new job
Christine has just quit a job that had many things she did not like, started a new job with many things she likes, and does not yet know about some other things that she will also like
Sally has just started her first job and likes many things about it and does not yet know about some other things that she will not like

questions.explanation: The **honeymoon effect** is when the old job's bad facets are gone, the new job's good facets are apparent and its bad facets are not yet known.

questions.prompt: If you have a friend who is experiencing the "honeymoon-hangover effect" what does this say about your friend's job satisfaction?

options.text: He/she was more satisfied on an old job than on a new job
He/she is just as satisfied on a new job as on an old job
His/her job satisfaction on a new job increases and then decreases
His/her job satisfaction on a new job increases and then stays at the same level
His/her job satisfaction on a new job decreases and then increases

questions.explanation: After a job change satisfaction rises (**honeymoon**) and then falls as the new job's bad facets are recognized (**hangover**).

questions.prompt: A large scale survey of values has shown that Americans rank slightly above the Japanese in the extent to which work is a central life interest.
questions.explanation: False. **Japan** topped the work-centrality list, while Americans were average, so Americans do not rank above the Japanese.

questions.prompt: According to Geert Hofstede's large survey, Japan is the most masculine society.
questions.explanation: True. **Japan** (along with Slovakia) is the most masculine society in Hofstede's research.

questions.prompt: According to Geert Hofstede's large survey, the United States is one of the most collective societies.
questions.explanation: False. The **United States** is among the most individualistic societies; Venezuela, Colombia and Pakistan are among the most collective.

questions.prompt: Equity theory is mainly concerned with distributive fairness rather than procedural fairness.
questions.explanation: True. **Equity theory** concerns distributive fairness, comparing outcome/input ratios, rather than the fairness of the process.

questions.prompt: According to equity theory, equity exists when work inputs equal work outputs.
questions.explanation: False. Equity exists when your **outcome/input ratio equals** the comparison person's ratio, not when your own inputs equal your outcomes.

questions.prompt: In highly collective cultures, allocating work rewards according to individual equity principles is the best way to promote job satisfaction.
questions.explanation: False. In collective cultures **equality of outcomes** or rewards tied to team performance may feel fairer than individual equity.

questions.prompt: The concept of organizational citizenship behaviour illustrates one good reason to cultivate the job satisfaction of the workforce.
questions.explanation: True. Satisfaction contributes strongly to **OCB**, which helps organizational effectiveness, so it is a good reason to cultivate satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Organizational citizenship behaviour refers to the idea of doing an excellent job in one's formally assigned responsibilities but not going beyond them.
questions.explanation: False. **OCB** is voluntary, informal behaviour that goes beyond the formally assigned job and contributes to organizational effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Organizational citizenship behaviour is explicitly recognized in most organizations' performance evaluation and reward systems.
questions.explanation: False. OCB is **unlikely to be picked up and rewarded** by the formal evaluation system, since it is not part of the job description.

questions.prompt: Contemporary thinking indicates that satisfaction causes performance when satisfaction is followed by rewards.
questions.explanation: False. It is **performance followed by rewards** that raises satisfaction. Contemporary research says satisfaction is more likely to affect performance than the reverse.

questions.prompt: In societies characterized by high power distance, organizations would tend to emphasize differences in rank and position.
questions.explanation: True. In high **power distance** societies inequality is accepted as natural and power differences are highlighted.

questions.prompt: More collective cultures tend to de-emphasize differences in power among their members.
questions.explanation: False. More collective cultures tend to **accentuate** power differences, while individualistic cultures downplay them.

questions.prompt: In equity theory terms, an unequal input/outcome ratio is an obvious example of procedural unfairness.
questions.explanation: False. An unequal input/outcome ratio is **distributive** unfairness; procedural fairness concerns the process used to decide outcomes.

questions.prompt: In an individualistic culture, distributing rewards according to equity principles rather than equality principles seems like a sensible strategy.
questions.explanation: True. Equity ties outcomes to individual contributions, which fits **individualistic** North American culture. Collective cultures may prefer equality.

questions.prompt: Values are a product of beliefs and attitudes.
questions.explanation: False. **Attitudes** are a product of beliefs and values, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Values usually change greatly from day to day.
questions.explanation: False. Values are broad, relatively **stable** preferences, and they do not change greatly from day to day.

questions.prompt: Theories of organizational behaviour, such as motivation, are easily transferred to all other cultures.
questions.explanation: False. OB theories from North America **might not translate well** to other cultures because of differences in values.

questions.prompt: The Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire measures attitudes.
questions.explanation: True. The **Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire** measures job satisfaction, an attitude, giving facet and overall measures.

questions.prompt: Beliefs are made up of values and attitudes.
questions.explanation: False. **Attitudes** are made up of beliefs and values; beliefs are not made up of values and attitudes.

questions.prompt: The Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire requires respondents to answer "yes" or "no" in describing whether a word or phrase describes particular facets of their jobs.
questions.explanation: The Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire's response format is not described in the 12th edition.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th edition names this questionnaire but does not describe its response format.

questions.prompt: According to equity theory, having outcomes equal to a comparison person does not guarantee equity.
questions.explanation: True. Equity depends on **ratios** of outcomes to inputs, so equal outcomes with unequal inputs still produce inequity.

questions.prompt: The job satisfaction facet that is most predictive of absenteeism is satisfaction with pay.
questions.explanation: False. Satisfaction with the **content of the work**, not pay, is the best predictor of absenteeism.

questions.prompt: The word discrepancy in discrepancy theory refers to the discrepancy between job inputs and job outcomes.
questions.explanation: False. The discrepancy is between the **job outcomes wanted and those perceived as received**, not between inputs and outcomes.

questions.prompt: Pay would not be considered an input in equity theory.
questions.explanation: True. **Pay is an outcome**, not an input; inputs include education, training, seniority and hard work.

questions.prompt: Job satisfaction does not contribute to performance.
questions.explanation: False. Job satisfaction is **associated with enhanced performance**, especially when it concerns the work itself.

questions.prompt: Intentions to quit are poor predictors of turnover.
questions.explanation: False. **Intentions to quit** are very good predictors of turnover.

questions.prompt: An employee attitude survey might sensibly use the Job Descriptive Index.
questions.explanation: True. The **Job Descriptive Index** is a well-developed satisfaction measure that firms could use in an attitude survey.

questions.prompt: Organizational commitment is the strength of the linkage between an employee and an organization.
questions.explanation: True. **Organizational commitment** is an attitude reflecting the strength of the linkage between an employee and an organization.

questions.prompt: Continuance commitment and normative commitment are caused by the same factors.
questions.explanation: False. **Continuance** commitment comes from costs of leaving or lack of alternatives, while **normative** comes from obligation or ideology.

questions.prompt: Emotions are intense, often long-lived, feelings caused by a particular event.
questions.explanation: False. Emotions are intense, often **short-lived** feelings caused by a particular event.

questions.prompt: Moods are not so intense, long-lived, and diffuse feelings.
questions.explanation: True. **Moods** are less intense, longer-lived and more diffuse than emotions.

questions.prompt: Affective events theory explains how emotions and moods affect job satisfaction.
questions.explanation: True. **Affective events theory** explains how emotions and moods, provoked by work events, affect job satisfaction.

questions.prompt: The tendency for moods and emotions to spread between people or throughout a group is known as emotional regulation.
questions.explanation: False. The tendency for moods and emotions to spread between people is **emotional contagion**, not emotional regulation.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition term: emotional labour.

questions.prompt: An example of emotional labour is when an employee is nice to a customer because he or she likes the customer.
questions.explanation: False. **Emotional labour** is following display rules despite how you feel, so being nice because you like the customer is not an example.

questions.prompt: Job satisfaction and organizational commitment are directly related to turnover intentions.
questions.explanation: True. **Job satisfaction and organizational commitment** both feed into turnover intentions in the turnover model.

questions.prompt: Employee job satisfaction does not translate into organizational profitability.
questions.explanation: False. Employee satisfaction **does translate into profitability**, through customer satisfaction and effective operations.

source.note: Corrected to match the text: shocks can prompt quitting even when someone is satisfied.

questions.prompt: Certain shocks like an earthquake might stimulate turnover despite satisfaction with one's current job.
questions.explanation: True. A **shock**, a sudden unexpected event, can stimulate turnover despite satisfaction with the current job. The text's examples include a marital breakup and an unsolicited job offer.

questions.prompt: Persuasion that is designed to modify or emphasize values is usually rationally oriented.
questions.explanation: Persuasion that targets values is emotionally oriented, whereas persuasion aimed at beliefs is rational.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: Persuasion strategies for changing values are not covered in the 12th edition chapter.

questions.prompt: If you want to change the values of a friend to be more like your own then you should focus on emotions.
questions.explanation: Changing a friend's values calls for emotional appeals rather than rational arguments.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: Persuasion strategies for changing values are not covered in the 12th edition chapter.

questions.prompt: If your boss is fair about the processes used to determine work outcomes you have interactional fairness.
questions.explanation: False. Fair processes are **procedural** fairness; interactional fairness is about respectful, informative communication.

questions.prompt: When your boss gives you respectful and informative communication about some outcome then you will have experienced interactional fairness.
questions.explanation: True. That is the definition of **interactional fairness**: respectful and informative communication about an outcome.

questions.prompt: It is impossible for absolutely fair outcomes or procedures to be perceived as unfair just because they are inadequately or uncaringly explained.
questions.explanation: False. Fair outcomes or procedures **can** be seen as unfair when inadequately or uncaringly explained, which is why interactional fairness matters.

questions.prompt: If you experience procedural unfairness you are most likely to be dissatisfied with your boss.
questions.explanation: False. Procedural unfairness mostly produces dissatisfaction with the **system**; interactional unfairness is more likely aimed at the boss.

questions.prompt: If you experience interactional unfairness you are most likely to be dissatisfied with your coworkers.
questions.explanation: False. Interactional unfairness is more likely to produce dissatisfaction with the **boss**, not with co-workers.

questions.prompt: Procedural and interactional fairness can offset the negative effects of distributive unfairness.
questions.explanation: True. Procedural and interactional fairness can, to some extent, **offset distributive unfairness**, though less so in less industrialized nations.

questions.prompt: People who are extraverted and high in neuroticism tend to be more satisfied with their jobs.
questions.explanation: False. People high in **neuroticism** are less satisfied; those who are extraverted and conscientious are more satisfied.

questions.prompt: People who are more optimistic and proactive report higher job satisfaction.
questions.explanation: True. More **optimistic and proactive** people report higher job satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Occupations with high cognitive demands tend to be paid more when the jobs are low in emotional labour.
questions.explanation: The link between cognitive demands, pay and emotional labour is not covered in the 12th edition.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The cognitive-demands and pay finding on emotional labour is not in the 12th edition.

questions.prompt: The connection between job satisfaction and good attendance probably stems in part from the tendency for job satisfaction to facilitate people's desire to want to come to work.
questions.explanation: The 12th edition explains the weak absence link through constraints on attendance rather than through a desire-to-attend mechanism.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: This explanation of the satisfaction-attendance link is not in the 12th edition.

questions.prompt: Certain shocks are most likely to stimulate turnover for employees who are dissatisfied with their jobs.
questions.explanation: False. **Shocks** can stimulate turnover despite satisfaction, so they are not limited to dissatisfied employees.

questions.prompt: If a friend of yours is aware of the good facets of a new job and knows that there are more good things on the horizon, he/she is experiencing the "honeymoon effect."
questions.explanation: False. In the **honeymoon effect** the new job's bad facets are not yet known; it does not involve knowing more good things are coming.

questions.prompt: When people experience the "hangover effect" their job satisfaction rises and then becomes stable.
questions.explanation: False. In the **hangover effect**, satisfaction with the new job decreases as its bad facets are recognized.

questions.prompt: After starting a new job, a friend of yours begins to realize some bad facets of the job in what is known as a "hangover effect."
questions.explanation: True. The **hangover effect** is the later decline in satisfaction as the new job's bad facets become apparent.

questions.prompt: Satisfaction with the content of work is the most important facet for absence from work and performance.
questions.explanation: True. Satisfaction with the **content of the work** is the best predictor of absenteeism and the most important facet for performance.

questions.prompt: In more feminine cultures, equality of outcomes might produce more feelings of distributive fairness than equity of outcomes.
questions.explanation: False. Equality of outcomes fits **collective** cultures; more feminine cultures may allocate by need rather than performance.

questions.prompt: People will endure a dissatisfying job if they are embedded in the community.
questions.explanation: True. Employees **embedded in the community** may endure a dissatisfying job rather than move.

questions.prompt: Procedural and interactional fairness are more critical for organizational citizenship behaviour than distributive fairness.
questions.explanation: True. **Procedural and interactional fairness** from a supportive manager are especially critical for OCB, though distributive fairness also matters.
